With just a few taps on a digital device, consumers can now have a wide range of items delivered straight to their doorstep in a matter of minutes. This on-demand economy, popularized by platforms like Amazon, Uber, and DoorDash, has rapidly extended into the restaurant industry. The meteoric rise indicates that the food delivery industry has turned it into a global market worth $150 billion [[1]] to reach $320 billion by 2029.
However, this convenience comes at a cost, with the planet left to pick up the tab. Behind the ease of enjoying a favorite meal lies an environmental burden. While couriers shuttle orders, their vehicles flood the streets, polluting the air and bringing about traffic congestion and carbon emissions. In fact, food delivery alone is [[2]] an estimated 3.6 million tons of CO₂ emissions annually. Households that spend just $63 per week on food delivery services generate a carbon footprint 450% higher than those that don’t, and [[3]], these customers aren’t in a small minority. Then, there is the issue of single-use plastics. Takeout meals are often bundled in plastic containers with tight-fitting lids or greasy wrappers, accompanied by straws and tiny condiment packets. When all these end up in landfills or oceans, the indecomposable materials in them [[4]] put wildlife in danger.
While the rise of food delivery provides unmatched convenience and boosts the restaurant industry, it also aggravates environmental problems. The new form of business is like [[5]]. As consumers and stakeholders in a shared planet, we must acknowledge the downside of our convenience-driven lifestyle and correct our course for a more sustainable future.

options.B: killing two birds with one stone
